The Daruma pond frog, Pelophylax porosus, is a medium-sized ranid endemic to Japan, where its reproductive biology has been studied across a range of thermal environments. Embryonic development proceeds rapidly in the warm waters typical of shallow rice paddies, with the age at first exogenous feeding recorded as 6 days [ab = 6 days] at 26 °C [T = 26 °C]. The newly emerged aquatic larva, or hatchling tadpole, possesses a negligible body mass, with a wet weight at birth estimated at 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams], a figure consistent with the small egg diameter of approximately 2 mm observed in this species. Following a period of intensive feeding and growth in the planktonic, filter-feeding tadpole stage, larval development culminates in metamorphosis. Under a controlled water temperature regime of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the time since birth at metamorphosis is approximately 70.15 days , a duration that aligns well with the developmental rates observed in other East Asian Pelophylax species.

Post-metamorphic juveniles emerge onto land as fully formed froglets, initiating the terrestrial juvenile phase of the life cycle. At this critical transition, the body length is relatively modest, with an average snout-vent length at metamorphosis of 2.7 cm . The corresponding wet weight at metamorphosis is approximately 2 grams , reflecting the loss of the water-rich tail and a shift to a more compact, terrestrial body plan, a value consistent with the pattern seen in other ranids of similar metamorphic size. This marked reduction in mass and associated morphological transformation, including gill resorption and skin keratinisation, allows the young frog to exploit a new suite of invertebrate prey. The juvenile growth period is characterized by a steady accumulation of biomass as the froglet feeds actively in the humid margins of ponds and streams, gradually approaching the adult size range.

Sexual maturation in Pelophylax porosus exhibits a pronounced sexual dimorphism in both timing and size, a pattern commonly documented across ranid frogs. Females, which mature later than males, reach puberty at a snout-vent length of approximately 5.76 cm [Lp = approximately 5.76 cm], whereas males, which undergo gametogenesis onset earlier, mature at a smaller body size of 4.3 cm [Lp = 4.3 cm]. This size disparity is linked to the energetic demands of egg production, as gravid females must accommodate a large clutch volume. The corresponding wet weight at puberty is approximately 19.5 grams [Wwp = approximately 19.5 grams] across both sexes, though individual variation is observed depending on local food availability. This pattern suggests that females allocate a greater proportion of their resources to achieving a larger body frame before first reproduction.
